newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra retreats from sex movie ban.
newsitem.headline: Canberra retreats from sex movie ban.

text.p: Australia's conservative government, stung by community outrage at parliament's recent abolition of a euthanasia law, on Tuesday dropped a plan to ban sex movies on pay television and video tape.

Attorney-General Daryl Williams said the government would ban movies that combined sex with violence, degradation or children, but the new policy failed to generally outlaw movies explicitly showing sex, as originally proposed.
The original proposal sparked criticism that Canberra for the second time in a month wanted to limit individual freedom and impose the moral views of politicians.
"Amazingly, commonsense prevailed," Fiona Patten, a spokeswoman for the sex video industry, told reporters.
Federal parliament last month struck down a pioneering territory law that allowed voluntary euthanasia, the world's first such law.

The conscience vote ignored the 70-percent majority of Australians who believed that terminally ill people should be allowed to kill themselves, and the decision was followed by a flood of protests to newspapers and talkback radio stations.
The government's standing in opinion polls has slumped since the euthanasia vote and newspaper commentators complained that with the movie ban the moralisers were at it again.
Its lead over the Labor opposition fell six percentage points in one poll published last week and Labor opposition on Tuesday was quick to back the cause of individual freedom over the sex movies.
"Labor believes that adults should be entitled to read, hear and see what they wish in private and in public," Labor communications spokesman Chris Schacht said in a statement.
His only concern was that people not be exposed to offensive, unsolicited material and that children be protected.
Sex videos are one of the biggest private industries in Canberra, Australia's political capital, which has been pushed into recession by the government's recent staffing cuts.
"I think that actually weighed very heavily in the cabinet's decision," Patten said. "Canberra has been hit very hard over the last 12 months with this new government."
